description: Earth, by Ear transforms NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into music, letting people hear our planet. Each frame becomes a four-second musical bar with a chord representing the image, a west-to-east melody, and sparkles for busy regions. Nine datasets, from night lights to ocean currents and lightning, each have unique musical voices. Explore using touch, mouse, or keyboard; compare moments in a duet; or take a guided tour.
summary: Earth, by Ear is an accessible “Earth Jukebox” that turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into music, so people can hear the planet instead of only seeing it. Press play and each frame of a visualization becomes a four-second bar: a chord for the overall picture, a melody that sweeps west to east, and a bright sparkle voice where the picture is busy. Nine EIC datasets, from night lights to ocean currents and lightning, each have their own musical voice. You can explore by mouse, touch or keyboard, compare two moments in a duet between your ears, or take a guided tour. Everything works with screen readers, and every track can be downloaded with a written description. It answers the challenge by pairing real EIC frames with sonification generated from their pixels. It matters because Earth science is shown mostly as pictures, which leaves out blind and low-vision people and anyone who learns by ear.
details:
What it does and how it works. The web app reads frames from NASA Scientific Visualization Studio / Earth Information Center animations and turns them into sound. Brighter regions play higher notes, snapped to a musical scale so the result is pleasant. Extreme values add tension (calm intervals become dissonant ones). Busy, high-contrast regions get more notes plus a sparkle voice. West to east becomes left to right in the stereo field. Each dataset has its own scale, home note and waveform.

  • Play this visualization: a whole animation becomes a short piece while a shaded band sweeps across the map.
  • Explore: every place you touch or point at plays its own note.
  • Duet: two moments play in your left and right ear, so a gap between the ears is the change.
  • Guided tour and planet’s chord: the tour picks striking places and describes them in words written from the data. The chord plays a whole map as one chord.

Benefits and impact. Blind and low-vision users can reach NASA Earth science that is mostly shown visually. Teachers, museums and the public get a new, emotional way to meet the data. Because the sound is rule-based, adding another visualization takes one import command.

Tools. Python (FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, OpenCV), ffmpeg, JavaScript with the Web Audio API (no libraries), HTML/CSS. An AI assistant (Claude) helped write and test the code and documentation.

Creativity. Our planet’s chord and duet ideas, tension that rises with extreme values, and rhythm that follows how busy the picture is. Sea-surface temperature uses each pixel’s colour along its blue-to-red ramp, not brightness, which suits a rainbow colour map better.

What we considered. Accessibility came first: keyboard control, spoken and written captions, vibration cues, and downloadable tracks with text descriptions. We were also honest about the data. Values are relative, read from pictures and not calibrated measurements. Globes and camera views report positions inside the frame, never invented latitude and longitude, and the empty sky is silent.
